Section 7: Common Student Pitfalls & Pro-Tips
• Confusing induction with conduction. Conduction: contact, same sign, rod loses
charge. Induction: no contact, opposite sign, rod keeps its charge. Tag which is
which before answering.
• Treating attraction as proof of charge. A charged object attracts neutral con-
ductors too. Only repulsion proves a body is charged. This single fact is tested
every year somewhere.
• Forgetting signs in additivity / sharing. The “share equally” rule uses the alge-
braic sum (𝑞1 + 𝑞2)/2. Plugging magnitudes loses the sign and the answer.
• Sloppy quantisation checks. A valid charge must give an integer when divided
by 𝑒. Always do that division to test “possible value” questions.
Pro-Tip: For “identical conductors touch” problems, jump straight to the av-
erage (𝑞1 + 𝑞2)/2 — and for 𝑁identical spheres brought into mutual contact
at once, each ends with (total charge)/𝑁. This collapses most charge-sharing
questions into one line. Always finish with a conservation check: total before
must equal total after.

Procedure B — Charging by conduction (contact). Touch a charged body to a neu-
tral conductor. Some charge flows across until they share it (equally, if identical). The
crucial signature: the neutral body acquires the same sign as the charging body, and
the charging body loses some of its charge.
Procedure C — Charging by induction (no contact). This is the most-tested proce-
dure. To induce a charge opposite to a charging rod on a neutral conductor: 1. Bring the
charged rod near (not touching) the neutral conductor. Free electrons rearrange: the
near side develops a charge opposite to the rod, the far side the same sign as the rod.
2. Earth the conductor (connect it to ground) while the rod stays in place. The like-sign
charge on the far side is repelled and flows away to earth. 3. Remove the earthing
first, while the rod is still near. The conductor is now left with only the unlike charge,
trapped by the rod’s attraction. 4. Remove the rod. The induced charge spreads over
the conductor.
The key reasoning: in induction the rod never loses any charge (no contact), and the
conductor ends up with charge opposite to the rod. Contrast this sharply with conduction,
where the rod does lose charge and the body gains the same sign.
Procedure D — The gold-leaf electroscope. A metal rod ends in two thin gold leaves
inside a glass case, topped by a metal disc. Touch a charged body to the disc: charge
spreads to both leaves, which acquire the same sign and repel each other, diverging.
The angle of divergence indicates how much charge is present — this is how charge is
detected and roughly measured.
Procedure E — Why we don’t notice quantisation. Since 𝑒= 1.6 × 10−19 C, even
a small everyday charge of 1 𝜇𝐶corresponds to 𝑛= 10−6/1.6 × 10−19 ≈6 × 1012
electrons. Adding or removing one electron changes this by one part in a trillion — utterly
undetectable — so charge seems to vary continuously, even though it does not.

4 · Continuous Charge Distribution
Exam Relevance: A bridge topic that powers most “field from an extended ob-
ject” problems. CBSE Boards ask for the definitions of linear/surface/volume
charge density and the integral set-up. JEE Main & Advanced lean on it heav-
ily — fields of rings, discs, arcs, and rods are perennial favourites, and the
charged-disc result connects directly to the infinite-sheet field from Gauss’s
law. NEET keeps it conceptual (symmetry-based zero-field arguments).
Section 1: Concept Intuition
Real charged objects — a metal wire, a plastic disc, a glass sphere — don’t carry a handful
of point charges.
They carry unimaginably many (recall 1 𝜇𝐶is already ∼6 × 1012
electrons). Tracking each one with Coulomb’s law is hopeless. So we do what physicists
always do with the very numerous: we stop counting individuals and start describing a
density.
Just as a city’s population is better described by “people per square kilometre” than by
listing every resident, a charged object is described by charge density — how much
charge sits per unit length, area, or volume. There are three flavours, depending on the
object’s shape: - Linear charge density 𝜆— for thin wires and rings (charge per metre).
- Surface charge density 𝜎— for sheets, discs, and shells (charge per square metre). -
Volume charge density 𝜌— for solid bodies (charge per cubic metre).
Think about it this way… Imagine spreading a fixed amount of ghee over a roti. If
you describe it as “grams per square centimetre,” you can find the ghee on any patch by
multiplying density by that patch’s area. Charge works identically: pick any tiny piece of
the object, and its charge is (density) × (size of the piece). That tiny charge, 𝑑𝑞, is small
enough to treat as a point charge — so Coulomb’s law applies to it — and the total field
is the vector sum (integral) of the contributions from all the pieces.
That is the entire game: chop the object into infinitesimal point-charge elements
𝑑𝑞, write the field 𝑑⃗𝐸of each, then add them up by integration, using symmetry to
kill the components that cancel.
Limiting Conditions & Assumptions. - The continuum (density) description is an ap-
proximation — valid because charge granularity (𝑒) is fantastically small compared to
the object. At truly atomic scales it breaks down. - The integral ∫𝑑𝑞/𝑟2 is straightfor-
ward only when symmetry makes most components cancel (rings, discs, arcs, infinite
lines/sheets). Without symmetry, the vector integral can be brutal. - Densities may be
uniform (constant) or non-uniform (a function of position); the set-up is the same, but
the integration differs.

Rub a plastic comb on dry hair and it suddenly picks up tiny bits of paper. Rub a glass
rod with silk and it attracts a hanging pith ball — but a second rod rubbed the same way

amber, ēlektron, gives us “electricity”), and they reveal the two foundational facts of this

transferring electrons. Remove electrons and an object is left positive; add electrons
and it becomes negative. Crucially, no new charge is ever created — it is only moved
around.

Think about it this way… Imagine a gulab jamun sitting inside a sealed box. The sugar
syrup it releases must all eventually escape through the box’s walls — the total amount

brutal integrals Coulomb’s law would demand.

Section 1: Concept Intuition
Real charged objects — a metal wire, a plastic disc, a glass sphere — don’t carry a handful
of point charges.
They carry unimaginably many (recall 1 𝜇𝐶is already ∼6 × 1012
electrons). Tracking each one with Coulomb’s law is hopeless. So we do what physicists
always do with the very numerous: we stop counting individuals and start describing a
density.
Just as a city’s population is better described by “people per square kilometre” than by
listing every resident, a charged object is described by charge density — how much
charge sits per unit length, area, or volume. There are three flavours, depending on the
object’s shape: - Linear charge density 𝜆— for thin wires and rings (charge per metre).
- Surface charge density 𝜎— for sheets, discs, and shells (charge per square metre). -
Volume charge density 𝜌— for solid bodies (charge per cubic metre).
Think about it this way… Imagine spreading a fixed amount of ghee over a roti. If
you describe it as “grams per square centimetre,” you can find the ghee on any patch by
multiplying density by that patch’s area. Charge works identically: pick any tiny piece of
the object, and its charge is (density) × (size of the piece). That tiny charge, 𝑑𝑞, is small

is the vector sum (integral) of the contributions from all the pieces.

𝑑𝑞, write the field 𝑑⃗𝐸of each, then add them up by integration, using symmetry to
kill the components that cancel.

conductor ends up with charge opposite to the rod. Contrast this sharply with conduction,
where the rod does lose charge and the body gains the same sign.

spreads to both leaves, which acquire the same sign and repel each other, diverging.

Rub a plastic comb on dry hair and it suddenly picks up tiny bits of paper. Rub a glass
rod with silk and it attracts a hanging pith ball — but a second rod rubbed the same way

and it becomes negative. Crucially, no new charge is ever created — it is only moved
around.

Exam Relevance: A bridge topic that powers most “field from an extended ob-
ject” problems. CBSE Boards ask for the definitions of linear/surface/volume
charge density and the integral set-up. JEE Main & Advanced lean on it heav-

Section 1: Concept Intuition
Real charged objects — a metal wire, a plastic disc, a glass sphere — don’t carry a handful
of point charges.
They carry unimaginably many (recall 1 𝜇𝐶is already ∼6 × 1012
electrons). Tracking each one with Coulomb’s law is hopeless. So we do what physicists
always do with the very numerous: we stop counting individuals and start describing a
density.
Just as a city’s population is better described by “people per square kilometre” than by
listing every resident, a charged object is described by charge density — how much
charge sits per unit length, area, or volume. There are three flavours, depending on the
object’s shape: - Linear charge density 𝜆— for thin wires and rings (charge per metre).
- Surface charge density 𝜎— for sheets, discs, and shells (charge per square metre). -
Volume charge density 𝜌— for solid bodies (charge per cubic metre).
Think about it this way… Imagine spreading a fixed amount of ghee over a roti. If
you describe it as “grams per square centimetre,” you can find the ghee on any patch by
multiplying density by that patch’s area. Charge works identically: pick any tiny piece of
the object, and its charge is (density) × (size of the piece). That tiny charge, 𝑑𝑞, is small
enough to treat as a point charge — so Coulomb’s law applies to it — and the total field
is the vector sum (integral) of the contributions from all the pieces.
That is the entire game: chop the object into infinitesimal point-charge elements
𝑑𝑞, write the field 𝑑⃗𝐸of each, then add them up by integration, using symmetry to
kill the components that cancel.
Limiting Conditions & Assumptions. - The continuum (density) description is an ap-
proximation — valid because charge granularity (𝑒) is fantastically small compared to
the object. At truly atomic scales it breaks down. - The integral ∫𝑑𝑞/𝑟2 is straightfor-
ward only when symmetry makes most components cancel (rings, discs, arcs, infinite
lines/sheets). Without symmetry, the vector integral can be brutal. - Densities may be
uniform (constant) or non-uniform (a function of position); the set-up is the same, but
the integration differs.
